item.description: A Japanese spacecraft rocketed toward Mars on Tuesday on a quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples.

item.title: Japan to launch world-first mission to moon of Mars
item.description: Japanese scientists will launch a spacecraft on Tuesday that aims to be the first to retrieve samples from one of Mars' moons, potentially helping unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.

item.title: Japan to launch historic round-trip mission to Mars moon
item.description: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars' moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.

item.title: Japan's MMX mission aims to swipe soil samples from Mars's moon Phobos
item.description: A Japanese space mission is about to launch towards Mars. But it will not land on the planet itself. Instead, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission will focus on Phobos, the bigger of Mars's two small moons.

item.title: Japan to launch spacecraft on a mission to get samples from a Martian moon
item.description: Japan is set to launch a spacecraft on the world's first mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of the two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting Mars.

item.title: Japan is launching a mission to Mars’s largest moon Phobos
item.description: The Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft, set to launch on 20 October, will bring back samples that should solve a moon mystery that has been vexing scientists for more than a century

item.title: Mars moon lander set to launch on 19 October
item.description: The Martian Moons eXploration ( MMX ) mission is set to launch into space on a H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 JST on 20 October 2026 (20:41 BST / 21:41 CEST on 19 October 2026). MMX will be the first mission to collect a sample from Mars’s moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth. item.title: The ESA's Euclid Space Telescope Has Discovered A New Comet
item.description: The ESA's Euclid space telescope was launched in July, 2026, and its mission is to observe billions of galaxies. The goal is to measure their redshifts over 10 billion years of Universal expansion, to better understand dark matter and dark energy. Surprisingly, the telescope has discovered a brand new comet, now named C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

item.title: Euclid discovers its first new comet 810 million miles from Earth
item.description: The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet in images taken between Sept. 16 and 24, 2026.

item.title: Euclid discovers new comet
item.description: The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, in images taken between 16 and 24 September 2026.

item.title: The Moon is Still Shrinking as it Cools. That Could Create a Hazard for Lunar Mission.
item.description: The Moon is slowly cooling and slowly shrinking. A study of its scarp faults calculates the rate of shrinkage, showing that it's extremely small. But the shrinking could still create landslides, a potential hazard for missions to the lunar surface.

item.title: NASA’s Simulated Mars Crew Marks One Year Inside Habitat
item.description: The four crew members in NASA’s simulated Mars mission have spent the past year living and working in isolation in a confined habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

Mars’s oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
item.description: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express , in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars’s most curious cloud.

item.title: Giant canyon on Mars is still tectonically active today
item.description: Scientists at Columbia University and Imperial College London have found that the largest canyon system in the solar system is still active and shaping Mars today, billions of years after it first formed.

item.title: Who speaks for Mars? Scientists call for ethical debate before terraforming begins
item.description: Transforming Mars into a more Earth-like world could irreversibly destroy scientific evidence about the planet's history and the possibility of extraterrestrial life. In an opinion article published in Eos, a team of Dutch, French and U.S. planetary scientists and ethicists warns that humanity risks destroying Mars' scientific record before it has been fully explored.

item.title: Simulations explore nuclear mitigation of asteroid threats
item.description: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) researchers are developing three-dimensional simulations to examine how a nuclear device could be used to deflect or potentially disrupt an asteroid threatening Earth.

item.title: First comprehensive Mars soil classification offers framework for exploration and future farming
item.description: A Ph.D. student at the University of Sydney has produced the first comprehensive classification system and map of Martian soils, creating a new framework that could help scientists compare landscapes across the Red Planet and identify promising locations for future exploration, habitation and food production.

item.title: The Perseverance Rover Reaches Another Milestone
item.description: NASA's Perseverance Rover has reached another milestone. It now holds the record for the longest distance travelled on another world, meaning Mars and Earth's Moon. It's all thanks the ingenuity behind AutoNav, it's hazard-detection driving system. It's a win for science, as more distance travelled means more scientific objectives are reached.

item.title: High-orbit satellites could light the way for travel to the moon
item.description: Acting as cooperative optical beacons, the satellites could provide GPS-like navigation and communications support for spacecraft operating across cislunar space.

item.title: Scientists pin down the origins of the moon’s tenuous atmosphere
item.description: The barely-there lunar atmosphere is likely the product of meteorite impacts over billions of years, a new study finds.

item.title: Study: Rocks from Mars’ Jezero Crater, which likely predate life on Earth, contain signs of water
item.description: The presence of organic matter is inconclusive, but the rocks could be scientists’ best chance at finding remnants of ancient Martian life.

item.title: Study determines the original orientations of rocks drilled on Mars
item.description: The “oriented” samples, the first of their kind from any planet, could shed light on Mars’ ancient magnetic field.
